title: The Platonic representation hypothesis: why different models converge
summary: Why separately trained models, even across vision and language, end up organizing the world alike: how representational similarity is measured, the 2024 Platonic representation hypothesis and its three pressures plus the co-occurrence argument, Balestriero and LeCun's JEPA proof that makes convergence a question of training views, and the critiques that shrink it once the evaluation set grows and the ruler is calibrated.

topics: deep dive: why different models converge — the Platonic representation hypothesis
concepts_taught: measuring representational similarity without matching neurons: kernels and similarity tables (RSA, CKA), mutual k-nearest-neighbor alignment with its ~k/n chance level, and model stitching as the run-it test

the Platonic representation hypothesis (Huh et al. 2024): strong vision models cluster, language-vision alignment rises with model competence (~0.16 max mutual-kNN on 1,024 WIT pairs); three pressures (multitask scaling, capacity, simplicity bias) and the idealized argument that contrastive learners converge to the world's pointwise-mutual-information kernel

Balestriero and LeCun's JEPA theorem: in an idealized world, separately trained modalities with shared positive pairs agree up to one rotation, next-token prediction only up to an invertible linear map; convergence as a property of good views (different observations of one scene) versus bad views (corruptions sharing nuisance)

the critiques: alignment collapsing as the evaluation gallery grows to millions and mutual-kNN's blindness to many-to-many correspondence (Back into Plato's Cave), and permutation-null calibration removing the global (CKA) scale trend while neighborhood agreement survives — the Aristotelian hypothesis of shared local neighborhoods
unsupervised embedding translation (vec2vec) as the practical edge of convergence: embeddings are not anonymized hashes
